depth: The depth map depicts a continuous ground plane that slopes upward into the distance, transitioning from a bright foreground roughly 1 m ahead of and below the camera wearer to a dark background more than 15–20 m away. The sidewalk boundary appears on the left, while a vertical tree trunk on the right draws nearer, changing from about 8 m away in frame 1 to roughly 4 m in frame 5. No people are visible. A small leashed dog stands directly ahead of and below the wearer at approximately 1.2–1.5 m—just outside arm’s reach—although the leash’s near end lies within reach at the bottom left. The dog is located 3–7 m in front of and left of the approaching trunk. In frame 5, the dog disappears completely beneath the lower edge, leaving only a tiny leash section in the bottom-left corner. Unlike the RGB strip’s uniformly white snow, this map reveals more clearly the snowbank’s smooth distance gradient, the small drop to the left-side sidewalk, and the precise 3D relief of the slender leash and tree trunks. Still, it is unreliable around the thin leash, whose thickness falsely blends into the neighboring snow surface, and across the distant upper-left street and houses beyond 15 m, where structural detail vanishes into flat black.
segmentation: Against its black background, the instance segmentation map separates only a handful of disconnected areas: the foreground dog, located 1–1.5 m ahead of and below the camera wearer in frames 1–3, plus distant upper-left background regions approximately 15–30 m away and about 14–28 m behind and left of the dog. Although the RGB view contains no people, the map incorrectly labels the dog as a “person” in frames 1 and 2, then as a “cat” in frame 3. It fails to detect the animal altogether in frame 4 when it crouches lower at 1 m, and likewise in frame 5 after it leaves through the bottom of the view. Along the upper-left street, parked vehicles and houses are inconsistently misidentified as tiny “person” instances in frame 1 and broad “train” masks in frames 3 and 4. In frame 5, however, three parked cars roughly 15–25 m away on the left are correctly marked as “car” instances; they form a curbside row and partly occlude one another. The masks in frames 1–3 sharply outline the animal’s initially rightward and subsequently leftward head direction, while frame 5 helps distinguish the overlapping distant cars from the dark street trees visible in RGB. Overall, though, the map is highly unreliable because of major class hallucinations, the total omission of the leash, trees, and snow, and the absence of any detections in frame 4.
pose: Across all five frames, the pose map is nearly solid black, showing only two small and incorrect yellow body skeletons in the lower foreground of frames 1 and 3, at the dog’s position roughly 1.2–1.5 m ahead of and below the camera wearer. No humans or visible hands occur within the view—the wearer’s hands holding the leash stay outside the frame beneath its lower edge—so there are no genuine human body orientations, gazes directed toward the camera, or person-to-person distances for the map to display. In frame 1, the erroneous skeleton runs vertically beside the left side of the dog’s back and its rightward-facing head. Frame 3 instead shows a small, folded yellow skeleton over the animal’s hunched torso while it faces forward-left. Frames 2, 4, and 5 have no pose detections whatsoever. The map therefore contributes no meaningful spatial detail beyond what is already visible in RGB and cannot be trusted: the estimator mistakenly responds to the dog’s dark outline against the white snow in two frames while failing to capture the scene’s real, non-human geometry.
